name.st: Child Helpline Lesotho (Mohala oa thuso oa bana)

description.en: Free, 24 hours. Parents, guardians and children can call to report violence against a child or to get counselling and referral.

contacts.evidence: gov.ls: 'The Child Helpline Lesotho operates 24-hours and it is a toll-free number that can be contacted by either the guardian, parent or children to report child violence cases. The child helpline toll-free number is 116.' Also listed as 'Child Helpline 116' on gov.ls home and socialdevelopment.gov.ls.
contacts.still_to_confirm: Confirm with the Ministry/UNICEF that 116 is currently staffed 24h on both mobile networks before any public release.

description.en: If a child or anyone is in immediate danger right now.

contacts.evidence: gov.ls home page 'Emergency Numbers' panel: 'National Emergency Line 112'. (Search snippets of lmps.org.ls/2026 also show 'Emergency Contact : 112', but that site was under maintenance when fetched, so gov.ls is the recorded source.)
contacts.still_to_confirm: Third-party travel sites list 123 for police; MEND did not use it. Confirm with LMPS which number reaches police fastest from rural districts.

name.en: Police - Child and Gender Protection Unit (CGPU)
name.st: Mapolesa - Child and Gender Protection Unit (CGPU)

description.en: The CGPU of the Lesotho Mounted Police Service handles cases involving children. You can also go to your nearest police station.

contacts.evidence: No official CGPU telephone number could be found: lmps.org.ls was 'under maintenance' on 2026-10-13. The unit's existence is documented (e.g. UNEG evaluation of the CGPU in all 11 districts), but no number is published by an official source MEND could reach.
contacts.still_to_confirm: Number to be confirmed with the Ministry and UNICEF

name.en: Ministry of Social Development - social workers / child protection
name.st: Lekala la Nts'etsopele ea Sechaba - basebeletsi ba sechaba

description.en: District social workers can help families and children who need care and protection.

contacts.evidence: socialdevelopment.gov.ls lists only administration/office numbers (e.g. Administration (+266) 22326371), not a child-protection or district social-worker line. gov.ls directory lists a different number (+266 22226004). Neither is a referral line and they disagree, so neither is shown to caregivers.

safety.note: Every free-text message is checked against these patterns BEFORE any other matching. A match always routes to the referral screen and never to advice. Patterns are deliberately broad: a false alarm (showing helpline numbers unnecessarily) is acceptable; a missed disclosure is not. Patterns are English only - a Sesotho safety lexicon must be built and tested with native-speaking child-protection staff. Categories are checked in order (most urgent first); the first match decides which contacts are listed first.

title.st: Ho halefa ha ngoana e monyenyane

text.en: All children misbehave at times. It is normal when they are tired, hungry, afraid, or learning to be independent.
First, look after yourself: give yourself a 10-second pause. Breathe in and out slowly five times, then respond more calmly.

steps.source_detail: Tip 4 'Take a Pause'; PLH handbook Session 8 building blocks ('use your calming strategies when ignoring a tantrum')

text.en: Try to redirect their attention first - offer something interesting, or say "Come, let's play a game together."

steps.source_detail: PLH Session 8: 'Try to redirect your child's attention first'; Tip 4 'Redirect'

text.en: If the tantrum is about demanding something, you can calmly ignore that one behaviour. Everyone at home should do the same. Be ready: it may get louder for a while before it stops.

steps.source_detail: PLH Session 8 building blocks (ignoring is a group effort; be prepared for agitation to grow)

text.en: As soon as the tantrum ends, praise the next good thing your child does - straight away.

steps.source_detail: PLH Session 8: 'When the bad behaviour ends, PRAISE the next positive behaviour immediately'

text.en: Daily one-on-one time, praise when they behave well, and consistent routines all reduce difficult behaviour. Notice when your child starts getting restless and distract them before it begins.

steps.source_detail: Tip 4 (One-on-One time, praise and routines reduce difficult behaviour; 'Stop it before it starts'); PLH Session 7 ('Be proactive! Catch the negative behaviour before it begins')

title.st: Ngoana oa ka ha a mamele

text.en: Children are much more likely to do what we ask when we tell them what TO do, and praise them when they get it right.
Say the behaviour you want to see: "Please put your clothes away" works better than "Don't make a mess".

steps.source_detail: Tip 2 'Say the behaviour you want to see'; UNICEF 'Set clear expectations'

text.en: Get their attention first: use their name, get down to their level, and speak in a calm voice. Give one instruction at a time, as a clear instruction rather than a question.

steps.source_detail: Tip 2 'It's all in the delivery'; PLH Session 5 building blocks

text.en: Be realistic. Can your child actually do what you are asking? Fifteen minutes of quiet is possible; a whole day is not.
Before switching activities, give a warning ("In five minutes we eat"). When they follow your instruction, praise them right away.

steps.source_detail: PLH Session 5 (transition warnings; praise when your child follows instructions)

text.en: Give a choice first: "If you don't pack away the toys now, there will be no toys after supper." Stay calm. If they still refuse, follow through - every time.

steps.source_detail: PLH Session 9 building blocks; Tip 4 'Use consequences'

text.en: Keep consequences short and realistic - taking a teenager's phone for one hour is easier to enforce than for a week. Afterwards, give your child a chance to do something good and praise them for it.
Parenting can be stressful, and you are not alone - millions of parents are trying and sometimes getting it wrong too. Taking care of yourself helps you support your children.

steps.source_detail: Tip 5 introduction ('Take care of yourself, so you can support your children'); UNICEF 'Praise yourself' ('Millions of parents across the world are all trying and we're all failing sometimes')

text.en: When you feel like screaming, take a pause: stop for 10 seconds and breathe in and out slowly five times. Parents around the world say this helps a lot.

label.st: Ntataise ka khefu ea motsotso o le mong

label.en: I'm afraid I might hurt my child
label.st: Ke tšaba hore nka utloisa ngoana oa ka bohloko

text.en: Sit comfortably, feet flat on the floor. Ask yourself: what am I thinking and feeling right now? Then listen to your breath going in and out - you can say to yourself "It's okay. I am okay." Notice your body and the sounds around you, then open your eyes.
Take a break when you can - when the children are asleep, do something you enjoy. You are not alone: find someone you trust to talk to about how you feel.

steps.source_detail: Tip 5 'Take a break' and 'You are not alone'

text.en: Each day, ask yourself: what is one thing I did well with my children today? Give yourself credit for it.

steps.source_detail: UNICEF 'Praise yourself'; Tip 3 'Praise yourself for what you did well today'

label.en: I'm afraid I might hurt my child
label.st: Ke tšaba hore nka utloisa ngoana oa ka bohloko

title.st: Thoriso le nako ea ho ba mmoho

text.en: One-on-one time is free. It helps children feel loved and secure, and shows them they are important. It can be 20 minutes a day - or even 5.
Switch off the TV and phone. Let your child choose the activity and lead the play, at their pace. Avoid criticising during this time.

label.en: Ideas for a baby or toddler

label.st: Mehopolo bakeng sa ngoana e monyenyane

text.en: With a baby or toddler: copy their faces and sounds, sing and make music with pots and spoons, stack cups, tell a story or look at pictures together.
With a young child: read or look at pictures, draw together, dance or sing, or turn a chore like cooking or cleaning into a game.
With a teenager: talk about something they like (music, sport, friends), cook a favourite meal together, or exercise together.
Praise your child when they behave well - even for things you expect, and even for trying. Give praise on its own, without adding a criticism. They may not show it, but they notice.

steps.source_detail: Tip 2 'Praise your child'; PLH Session 4 building blocks

text.en: Rules and routines give children a sense of security. A flexible but consistent daily routine, with time for activities and free time, can help children feel more secure and behave better.

steps.source_detail: PLH Session 6 building blocks; Tip 3 'Create a flexible but consistent daily routine'

text.en: Let children help plan the routine. They follow it better when they helped make it.
Make house rules when everyone is calm, not in the middle of a problem. Keep each rule clear and specific, and praise your child when they follow it.

label.st: Mehopolo ea nako ea ho robala

text.en: A regular bedtime routine can help - for example: wash, brush teeth, bedtime clothes, a story, then sleep. Not enough sleep can make a child cranky the next day.

steps.source_detail: PLH Session 8 home activities (bedtime routine example); Session 6 building blocks (sleep)

text.en: At the end of each day, tell your child one positive or fun thing they did.
A good connection with your teen is the base for supporting them. Show interest in what matters to them, share things about yourself, and ask for their opinions.
Listen actively: look at them, nod, and don't judge - even when you disagree. Ask open questions like "Why do you think you got upset when...?"
Repeat back what you heard ("What I hear you saying is...") and accept their feelings: "It's understandable that you're angry - I would feel the same."

label.st: Ha a batle ho bua le 'na

text.en: Don't force the conversation. Let them know you are there and ready to listen any time. Share funny things and good news too - laughing together builds the relationship.
Ask your teen to help make the household rules and agree on the consequences. Being involved shows them you see them growing into independent people.

title.st: Mekhoa e meng ntle le ho otla

text.en: Parents often shout or hit because they are stressed and don't see another way. The evidence is clear: shouting and hitting do not work and can do more harm than good in the long run.

steps.source_detail: UNICEF 'Why positive discipline?' (paraphrasing Prof. Lucie Cluver)

text.en: In the moment: take a pause. Ten seconds, five slow breaths, then respond. Remember - there are no bad children, only bad behaviour.

steps.source_detail: Tip 4 'Take a Pause'; UNICEF; PLH Session 7 ('Children are good. Behaviours can be bad.')

text.en: Calm consequences teach responsibility and are more effective than hitting or shouting. Explain the consequence first and give your child the chance to change.
If they don't stop, follow through calmly, without anger. If they do stop, give them lots of praise.

label.en: I'm afraid I might hurt my child
label.st: Ke tšaba hore nka utloisa ngoana oa ka bohloko

text.en: Prevention works best: daily one-on-one time, praise for good behaviour, clear instructions, and distraction when you see trouble coming. Give simple jobs your child can do, and praise them when they do it.
